answers.answer: He left Bistritz by coach on the evening of 4 May (St George's Eve) and reached the castle a little after midnight, so he arrived in the early hours of 5 May. His journal records it under 5 May ('5 May. The Castle').

Dr John Seward. He was one of Lucy's suitors and her doctor, and Van Helsing was his 'old friend and master' from Amsterdam, someone he had known for years. Seward wrote asking him to come and see Lucy (2 September). Arthur had not met Van Helsing before 7 September.

The question's premise is wrong. On 30 September nothing was attacking Lucy. She had died around 20 September, and her Un-Dead body was staked and laid to rest on the night of 29 September. At the council on 30 September the group's belief was about what had preyed on her: a vampire, the Count ('this vampire which is amongst us'), whom Van Helsing says he would have stopped had he known, so that 'one so precious life had been spared'. Their task now was to find and destroy him.

(1) Lucy's illness. On 2 September he found 'not any functional disturbance or any malady that I know of' and took it for an ordinary medical case, then sent for Van Helsing. He gave that view up when Van Helsing explained the vampire theory (26 September). (2) The idea that Lucy was Un-Dead. At first he called Van Helsing mad (26 September), and he explained away the empty coffin as body-snatchers and the child as unwounded. On 27 September he saw Lucy's body blooming a week after death, with sharper teeth, and was 'almost willing to accept'. On 28 September he went back on that, called the ideas 'outrages on common sense' and suspected Van Helsing was unhinged or had done it himself. He was finally convinced on 29 September when he saw the Un-Dead Lucy in the churchyard with a child. (3) Renfield's sanity. On 1 October he refused Renfield's sane, earnest plea to be sent away and treated it as a mad fit. He revised this on 3 October, when the dying Renfield said he had been 'as sane then' and that the Count had come to his window. (4) Not a retraction but a related point: he joined the decision to keep Mina out of the work 'for her safety', and this was overtaken after the Count attacked her on 3 October. This list is my reading of the evidence, not a list the text gives.

Fifty boxes of earth: Harker saw 'fifty in all' at the castle. Twenty-one were later moved out of Carfax, so 29 stayed in the Carfax chapel, and the hunters sterilised those with the Host on 3 October. Of the 21: six went to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town, and six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey, and Godalming and Morris destroyed both lots. Nine went to the house in Piccadilly, where eight were found and sterilised. The Count escaped with the ninth on the Czarina Catherine to Galatz, and it was carried toward the castle. He was killed lying in that box on 6 November.

26 July 1893, in Mina Murray's journal at Whitby. Mina writes that Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep'. Mrs Westenra had told her about it and said Lucy's father had the same habit, so they agreed Mina would lock their door every night. No earlier passage mentions it.

Only one: her diary entry of 12 September ('How good they all are to me... Good-night, everybody'). It names no Arthur, Holmwood or Godalming. All her other records name him: the 'Wednesday' letter (May), the 24 May letter, the 30 August Whitby letter, and the diary entries of 24 August, 25 August, 9 September and 17 September. Her 17 September memorandum also names him, in its closing 'Good-bye, dear Arthur'. This was checked by name only; a pronoun reference to him would not show up.
In Jonathan Harker's journal, in the entry dated 5 May. The Count says it on Harker's first night at the castle, after supper, in the small hours after his arrival around midnight.

experience: The exact tools did most of the deciding. `list --source Lucy --with/--without Arthur` answered Q7 almost on its own, and `grep "children of the night"` answered Q8 in one call. `list` with a date window ('62 passages match (18 entries)') showed me the 29 to 30 September timeline at a glance. That is how I saw that Lucy had already been staked, so Q3 rests on a false premise. The CONTINUES warning was useful the first time: `around e0006.4` took me to the 5 May headings and the 'within a few minutes of midnight' line I needed for Q1. After that it fired on almost every result and turned into noise. Some warnings misled me or got in the way. `search "the last box of earth taken on board the ship Czarina Catherine"` was REFUSED with 'ERROR SUPERLATIVE: An extreme needs the whole matching set'. The word 'last' was descriptive there, not a superlative, so I had to rephrase. On 30 September, OFF_QUESTION flagged e0161.1, but that passage was the best evidence for Q3. TIME_SKEW fired on searches I had deliberately date-filtered. FRONTIER_EXPLOSION and OPINION on Q4 told me nothing I could act on. One inconsistency: `grep "walking in her sleep"` returned '0 passages match', while `grep "her sleep"` found the passage containing that exact phrase. I suspect a quote or whitespace difference, and it nearly made me miss the true first mention. I wish the tool had said when a grep ran on normalised text. I also wish a warning could tell a filter I chose apart from a skew it detected, and that `list` showed which entries are letters and which are diaries.
